notes.title: Design cycle in context
paragraphs: The design cycle connects inquiry, development, creation and evaluation through decisions supported by evidence. It is not a rule that each stage happens only once. A failed usability test may reveal an unclear requirement, sending the designer back to inquiry before making another prototype. Keep the problem separate from a favoured solution so alternatives remain possible. At each transition, record what was learned and why the next action follows. A finished object is evidence of making; meeting the agreed criteria requires separate evaluation.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: a classroom sign is attractive, but four of six visitors cannot find the collection tray. Decide the next design step.
steps: The finding concerns navigation, so appearance alone does not demonstrate success.
Observe where visitors look and compare the sign’s wording and placement before revising a prototype.
workedExamples.conclusion: Return to the evidence behind the navigation requirement, then test a targeted change with the same task.

flashcards.front: Why can a design stage be revisited?
flashcards.back: New evidence can reveal a problem in an earlier assumption or decision.

flashcards.front: How does an object differ from an evaluated outcome?
flashcards.back: The object shows it was made; evaluation checks it against requirements.

flashcards.front: Why separate problem and solution?
flashcards.back: It keeps alternative ways of meeting the need open.

flashcards.front: What belongs in a decision record?
flashcards.back: Evidence, the decision it supports and the next action.

diagrams.title: Design cycle: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Inquiry → Development → Evaluation. A selected revision must face the original user task.

nodes.label: Evaluation
nodes.detail: Test whether visitors now find it unaided.

edges.label: Observed difficulty directs alternative ideas.
A selected revision must face the original user task.

additionalPractice.prompt: A team says “We completed the cycle because we built the model.” Explain the missing evidence.
hints: Ask whether the need was met.
solution: The model demonstrates creation.
The team still needs tests against its specifications.
It should use results to evaluate success and identify any justified revision.
successCriteria: The model demonstrates creation.
The team still needs tests against its specifications.
It should use results to evaluate success and identify any justified revision.

additionalPractice.prompt: A prototype passes a size test but confuses users. Explain why returning to research is reasonable.
solution: Passing the size criterion establishes only fit.
Observed confusion suggests a usability need remains unresolved.
Further observation can identify whether labels, arrangement or instructions need revision.
successCriteria: Passing the size criterion establishes only fit.
Observed confusion suggests a usability need remains unresolved.
Further observation can identify whether labels, arrangement or instructions need revision.

notes.title: Prototyping in context
paragraphs: A prototype is built to answer a question at a chosen level of detail. A paper screen can test whether labels make sense without implementing a database. A card mock-up can test reach and arrangement without proving final strength. State the uncertainty before choosing materials or fidelity. Keep features irrelevant to the test simple so time is spent on what the result can actually establish. Record limitations explicitly: success with a simplified model does not automatically transfer to a finished product with different dimensions, materials or interaction.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional task: test whether a new user understands three menu labels before programming an app.
steps: Create paper screens with the proposed labels and a realistic task, such as finding the next club meeting.
Ask a participant to choose a route without coaching, recording wrong turns and comments.
workedExamples.conclusion: The prototype can reveal label and navigation problems, but it does not test loading speed or real data storage.

flashcards.front: What should determine prototype fidelity?
flashcards.back: The uncertainty the prototype needs to investigate.

flashcards.front: What can a paper interface test?
flashcards.back: Labels, task flow and some navigation decisions.

flashcards.front: What can it not establish by itself?
flashcards.back: Technical performance, real data handling or all final interaction behaviour.

flashcards.front: Why avoid coaching during a usability trial?
flashcards.back: Coaching can hide the difficulty the prototype is meant to reveal.

diagrams.title: Prototyping: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Uncertainty → Prototype → Observation. The task produces evidence about the chosen uncertainty.

nodes.label: Prototype
nodes.detail: Paper screens with clickable choices simulated by hand.

edges.label: The question determines which features need representation.
The task produces evidence about the chosen uncertainty.

additionalPractice.prompt: A foam chair model is used to claim the final chair is safe under load. Evaluate.
solution: The foam model may represent shape or scale.
It does not establish the load-bearing behaviour of the final materials and joints.
A suitable strength evaluation under appropriate supervision is needed before making a safety claim.
successCriteria: The foam model may represent shape or scale.
It does not establish the load-bearing behaviour of the final materials and joints.
A suitable strength evaluation under appropriate supervision is needed before making a safety claim.

additionalPractice.prompt: A team spends hours colouring a prototype intended only to test label clarity. Suggest a better allocation.
solution: Keep labels readable and the layout realistic enough for the task.
Use simple visual styling where colour is not part of the test question.
Spend the saved time observing several users and revising ambiguous wording.
successCriteria: Keep labels readable and the layout realistic enough for the task.
Use simple visual styling where colour is not part of the test question.
Spend the saved time observing several users and revising ambiguous wording.

notes.title: Problem identification in context
paragraphs: A design problem describes a gap between a user’s current experience and a desired outcome. It should identify who is affected, in what situation and with what observable difficulty. Avoid turning the first proposed solution into the problem itself: “we need an app” does not explain the unmet need. Separate direct observations from interpretations about motives. A small sample can reveal a useful issue without proving that every user experiences it. A bounded brief makes constraints visible and gives later evaluation a clear purpose.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional observations: five of eight pupils leave worksheets in the wrong collection tray; two trays have similar labels. Write a problem statement.
steps: Identify users and task: pupils submitting worksheets need to distinguish the correct tray.
State the observed difficulty and limit: five of eight observed submissions were misplaced, and similar labels are a possible cause to investigate.
workedExamples.conclusion: The brief concerns reliable worksheet submission; it does not prematurely require a digital system.

flashcards.front: What makes a problem user-centred?
flashcards.back: It describes a user, situation and unmet need.

flashcards.front: Why is “build an app” not a full problem statement?
flashcards.back: It names a solution without establishing the difficulty.

flashcards.front: How should a possible cause be phrased?
flashcards.back: As a hypothesis to investigate unless evidence already establishes it.

flashcards.front: What does a bounded brief include?
flashcards.back: The need, intended users, context and relevant constraints.

diagrams.title: Problem identification: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Observation → Need → Open brief. The need guides solutions without choosing one prematurely.

nodes.label: Observation
nodes.detail: Five of eight submissions are misplaced.

nodes.label: Open brief
nodes.detail: Improve submission clarity within the classroom constraints.

edges.label: The error pattern identifies a practical difficulty.
The need guides solutions without choosing one prematurely.

additionalPractice.prompt: Rewrite “The school needs a robot” as a useful inquiry question for a fictional problem of lost library books.
solution: Ask where and when returned books become difficult to locate.
Identify which users need to find them and what delays occur.
Investigate ways to improve tracking before deciding whether any robot is appropriate.
successCriteria: Ask where and when returned books become difficult to locate.
Identify which users need to find them and what delays occur.
Investigate ways to improve tracking before deciding whether any robot is appropriate.

additionalPractice.prompt: Two users report difficulty; a brief says “All users hate the product.” Correct the evidence claim.
solution: Two users reported a specific difficulty.
The evidence does not establish every user’s experience or hatred.
Record the difficulty accurately and investigate its frequency with a broader suitable sample.
successCriteria: Two users reported a specific difficulty.
The evidence does not establish every user’s experience or hatred.
Record the difficulty accurately and investigate its frequency with a broader suitable sample.

notes.title: Research in context
paragraphs: Design research should answer decisions the brief actually requires. Observation can reveal what users do, while an interview can explore how they explain their experience; neither automatically replaces the other. Product analysis can identify existing approaches, but copying an attractive feature without understanding its context is weak evidence. Record source, date, method and limitations so findings can be traced. Prefer questions that invite an account of behaviour over leading questions that seek agreement. Collect only information needed for the design task and avoid recording unnecessary personal details.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional inquiry: users struggle to locate a timetable on a club noticeboard. Plan two complementary research methods.
steps: Observe a small group attempting to find a specified meeting time, recording search paths and completion.
Ask afterwards which labels or visual cues they expected, without suggesting that a particular colour is the answer.
workedExamples.conclusion: Observation reveals task behaviour; the follow-up interview helps explain expectations while remaining a self-report.

flashcards.front: What can observation reveal?
flashcards.back: Actions and difficulties during a task.

flashcards.front: What can an interview add?
flashcards.back: A user’s explanation, expectations and priorities.

flashcards.front: What is a leading question?
flashcards.back: A question that steers the respondent towards a preferred answer.

flashcards.front: Why record research limitations?
flashcards.back: They define how far the finding can support a design decision.

diagrams.title: Research: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Decision need → Methods → Evidence. Different methods illuminate different parts of the problem.

nodes.label: Decision need
nodes.detail: Which cues help users find a timetable?

nodes.label: Methods
nodes.detail: Observe a task, then ask about expectations.

edges.label: The decision determines what to investigate.
Different methods illuminate different parts of the problem.

additionalPractice.prompt: Improve “Wouldn’t a larger button be much better?” as an interview question.
solution: Ask: “How did you decide where to press?”
Follow with: “Was any part difficult to identify?”
These questions allow the user to describe the problem before proposing a button size.
successCriteria: Ask: “How did you decide where to press?”
Follow with: “Was any part difficult to identify?”
These questions allow the user to describe the problem before proposing a button size.

additionalPractice.prompt: A designer uses one old product review as proof that current users need a feature. Evaluate.
hints: Ask what current evidence is missing.
solution: The review records one person’s experience at a particular time.
The product and user context may differ from the present brief.
Use it as a lead for current user research rather than conclusive proof.
successCriteria: The review records one person’s experience at a particular time.
The product and user context may differ from the present brief.
Use it as a lead for current user research rather than conclusive proof.

notes.title: Specifications in context
paragraphs: A specification translates a need into a requirement that can be checked. State the feature or performance, threshold, conditions and method of verification. Separate mandatory constraints from preferences so a strong optional feature cannot conceal a critical failure. Include units where a quantity is measured and define ambiguous words such as easy or durable. Thresholds should come from the brief, research or a justified design decision, not be invented after seeing results. Keep the same requirement version attached to its test record.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional brief: a display must fit a 240 mm shelf with 15 mm clearance at each side. Write a maximum-width requirement.
steps: Total reserved clearance is 15 + 15 = 30 mm.
Maximum display width is 240 − 30 = 210 mm; measure the widest point after assembly.
workedExamples.conclusion: The assembled display must be no wider than 210 mm, checked with a suitable ruler at its widest point.

flashcards.front: What makes a requirement testable?
flashcards.back: A defined feature, threshold, conditions and check.

flashcards.front: Why distinguish mandatory and preferred requirements?
flashcards.back: An optional advantage cannot compensate for violating a mandatory constraint.

flashcards.front: When should thresholds be set?
flashcards.back: Before testing, using the brief or justified research.

flashcards.front: Why include units?
flashcards.back: They make quantities unambiguous and comparable.

diagrams.title: Specifications: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Available space → Clearance → Requirement. The remaining space becomes a measurable maximum.

edges.label: Subtract both side clearances.
The remaining space becomes a measurable maximum.

additionalPractice.prompt: A 300 mm opening needs 12 mm clearance on each side. Calculate the maximum object width.
solution: Total clearance is 2 × 12 = 24 mm.
Maximum width is 300 − 24 = 276 mm.
Specify an assembled width no greater than 276 mm under the stated brief.
successCriteria: Total clearance is 2 × 12 = 24 mm.
Maximum width is 300 − 24 = 276 mm.
Specify an assembled width no greater than 276 mm under the stated brief.

additionalPractice.prompt: Improve “The instructions must be clear” using a fictional test of five first-time users.
hints: Name a task and a threshold.
solution: A possible specification is: at least four of five first-time users complete the three-step setup without hints.
Observe the defined task using the same instructions.
Record each completion and any help rather than relying only on users saying the text is clear.
successCriteria: A possible specification is: at least four of five first-time users complete the three-step setup without hints.
Observe the defined task using the same instructions.
Record each completion and any help rather than relying only on users saying the text is clear.

notes.title: Ideation in context
paragraphs: Ideation explores alternative ways to meet a need before committing to one solution. Vary the principle, arrangement or interaction, not only colours on the same concept. Compare ideas against the same criteria and explain why those criteria matter. Weighted scores can organise a decision, but their result depends on the weights and the meaning of the scale. Apply mandatory constraints before ranking preferences. A score is a decision aid rather than proof of objective superiority; close results or uncertain ratings may justify another prototype test.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional concepts pass all mandatory constraints. Weight readability by 3 and portability by 1. A scores 4 and 2; B scores 3 and 5 on a higher-is-better scale. Compare.
steps: The weighted tie means this scoring scheme does not distinguish the concepts; inspect the trade-off or test uncertain ratings.
workedExamples.conclusion: Neither concept wins under the stated weights. A favours readability; B favours portability.

flashcards.front: What makes ideas meaningfully different?
flashcards.back: They vary an approach, arrangement or interaction relevant to the need.

flashcards.front: What should happen before preference scoring?
flashcards.back: Check mandatory constraints.

flashcards.front: What does a weighted score depend on?
flashcards.back: The selected criteria, weights, scale and ratings.

flashcards.front: How should a tie be handled?
flashcards.back: Examine trade-offs or gather better evidence rather than inventing a winner.

diagrams.title: Ideation: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Alternatives → Common criteria → Decision. The result directs further investigation rather than forcing certainty.

nodes.label: Common criteria
nodes.detail: Apply the same weights and scale.

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.detail: A tie requires a justified further step.

edges.label: Common criteria make the comparison consistent.
The result directs further investigation rather than forcing certainty.

additionalPractice.prompt: Usability weight 2, material use weight 1; higher scores are better. A scores 5 and 2, B scores 4 and 3. Calculate and interpret.
hints: Multiply each score by its weight.
solution: A scores 2 × 5 + 2 = 12.
B scores 2 × 4 + 3 = 11.
A ranks higher under these weights, provided both pass mandatory constraints.
successCriteria: A scores 2 × 5 + 2 = 12.
B scores 2 × 4 + 3 = 11.
A ranks higher under these weights, provided both pass mandatory constraints.

additionalPractice.prompt: A concept wins a preference score but exceeds the maximum permitted width. Should it be selected unchanged?
hints: Distinguish a constraint from a preference.
solution: It fails a mandatory size constraint.
A higher preference score does not cancel that failure.
Revise it to fit and reassess, or choose a compliant alternative.
successCriteria: It fails a mandatory size constraint.
A higher preference score does not cancel that failure.
Revise it to fit and reassess, or choose a compliant alternative.

notes.title: Testing in context
paragraphs: A test turns a requirement into a repeatable observation. Specify the task, conditions, participants or samples, measurements and success rule before collecting results. Keep assistance consistent: a hinted completion may not count as an unaided success. Record failures and incomplete trials rather than silently removing them. Repeated measurements can reveal variation, but a small classroom trial does not establish performance for every user. If conditions change, label the new test clearly so differences in results are not automatically attributed to the design revision.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional rule: four of six users must find a label within 30 seconds without hints. Times are 18, 24, 31, 22, 28 and 35 seconds; the 22-second attempt used a hint.
steps: Unaided successes within 30 seconds are 18, 24 and 28: three users.
The 22-second attempt fails the unaided condition, and 31 and 35 exceed the time limit.
workedExamples.conclusion: The result is three of six, so the four-of-six criterion is not met.

flashcards.front: Why define the success rule first?
flashcards.back: It prevents changing the target to suit the results.

flashcards.front: Does a hinted completion count as unaided?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Why keep failed trials?
flashcards.back: They are part of the evidence about performance.

flashcards.front: What can changing test conditions confound?
flashcards.back: Whether a difference came from the design or the changed conditions.

diagrams.title: Testing: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Rule → Classification → Judgement. The count is compared with the pre-set threshold.

nodes.label: Judgement
nodes.detail: Three of six is below the required four.

edges.label: Each observation is checked against both conditions.
The count is compared with the pre-set threshold.

additionalPractice.prompt: A test requires five of five objects to fit. Four fit and one jams. Evaluate the claim “80%, so it passed”.
hints: Do not replace it after testing.
solution: Four of five equals 80%.
The stated rule requires all five, or 100%.
The design fails that criterion despite most objects fitting.
successCriteria: Four of five equals 80%.
The stated rule requires all five, or 100%.
The design fails that criterion despite most objects fitting.

additionalPractice.prompt: A second trial uses easier tasks and shows faster times. Can the improvement be attributed solely to the design?
solution: Task difficulty changed alongside the design.
Faster times may reflect the easier task.
Retest comparable tasks under consistent conditions before attributing the difference solely to the revision.
successCriteria: Task difficulty changed alongside the design.
Faster times may reflect the easier task.
Retest comparable tasks under consistent conditions before attributing the difference solely to the revision.

notes.title: Evaluation in context
paragraphs: Evaluation compares an outcome with requirements using recorded evidence. State which criteria pass, fail or remain untested, and explain the significance of each result. Do not average away a critical failure by counting several minor successes. User comments can explain a problem, but measured performance may challenge a positive opinion. Distinguish evidence about the prototype from claims about production use. A useful evaluation ends with a justified priority for improvement and a clear account of what a new test would need to establish.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional organiser criteria: width at most 160 mm, cost at most £8, and all six labels readable at the test distance. Results: 155 mm, £7.20 and five readable labels.
steps: The width and cost satisfy their thresholds.
Five of six labels does not meet an all-six readability requirement.
workedExamples.conclusion: The organiser meets two criteria but needs a readability revision before it can be said to meet the whole specification.

flashcards.front: What are the three useful criterion statuses?
flashcards.back: Met, not met and not yet tested.

flashcards.front: Can several minor successes cancel a critical failure?
flashcards.back: No; evaluate the role of each requirement.

flashcards.front: Why separate prototype and final-product claims?
flashcards.back: Materials, scale and use conditions may differ.

flashcards.front: What makes an improvement justified?
flashcards.back: It addresses a specific evidenced weakness.

diagrams.title: Evaluation: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Results → Criteria comparison → Priority. The unmet requirement determines the next revision.

nodes.label: Criteria comparison
nodes.detail: Size and cost pass; readability fails.

nodes.label: Priority
nodes.detail: Repair the unreadable label and retest.

edges.label: Each result is compared with its own threshold.
The unmet requirement determines the next revision.

additionalPractice.prompt: A user says “I love it” but cannot complete the required task. How should both findings be reported?
hints: Preference and task success are different measures.
solution: Report the positive preference accurately.
Record the unsuccessful task completion separately.
Do not treat liking the design as evidence that it meets the usability requirement.
successCriteria: Report the positive preference accurately.
Record the unsuccessful task completion separately.
Do not treat liking the design as evidence that it meets the usability requirement.

additionalPractice.prompt: A design has not been tested outdoors. Evaluate “It works in all weather”.
solution: The claim exceeds the test evidence.
Indoor performance does not establish outdoor or all-weather behaviour.
Report the conditions actually tested and identify outdoor testing as unresolved.
successCriteria: The claim exceeds the test evidence.
Indoor performance does not establish outdoor or all-weather behaviour.
Report the conditions actually tested and identify outdoor testing as unresolved.

notes.title: Iteration in context
paragraphs: Iteration is a purposeful change linked to a previous observation. Record the version, issue, proposed mechanism of improvement and test result. Changing several features at once may improve the product but makes it harder to identify which change mattered. Keep an earlier version or a clear record so comparisons remain possible. A revision is not automatically an improvement: it can solve one problem while creating another. Retest the affected criterion and any constraints the change might disturb, such as dimensions, cost or accessibility.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional v1: users confuse two identical folder tabs. V2 adds distinct text labels without changing size. Plan the comparison.
steps: Keep the filing task and instructions comparable, and record unaided correct selections.
Compare v1 and v2 results while checking that the added text remains readable at the required size.
workedExamples.conclusion: The change has a stated mechanism;distinguishable labels;but its benefit remains a testable claim until results are collected.

flashcards.front: What connects an iteration to evidence?
flashcards.back: A specific observed issue and a proposed reason the change should help.

flashcards.front: Why keep version records?
flashcards.back: They allow changes and results to be traced.

flashcards.front: Is every revision an improvement?
flashcards.back: No; it can fail or introduce new problems.

flashcards.front: What should be retested?
flashcards.back: The affected requirement and any constraints the change may disturb.

diagrams.title: Iteration: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Observed issue → Revision → Retest. The proposed improvement must be checked in the same kind of task.

edges.label: The confusion suggests a need for distinguishable cues.
The proposed improvement must be checked in the same kind of task.

additionalPractice.prompt: A revision changes colour, wording and location, then task success rises. What can be concluded?
hints: Separate overall outcome from individual causes.
solution: The revised combination performed better in that trial.
The result does not isolate which of the three changes caused the difference.
A controlled follow-up can examine individual changes if that causal question matters.
successCriteria: The revised combination performed better in that trial.
The result does not isolate which of the three changes caused the difference.
A controlled follow-up can examine individual changes if that causal question matters.

additionalPractice.prompt: A larger handle improves grip but makes the product too wide. Evaluate the iteration.
solution: The grip result supports one improvement.
The increased width violates another constraint.
Further revision is needed to preserve the grip benefit while restoring compliance.
successCriteria: The grip result supports one improvement.
The increased width violates another constraint.
Further revision is needed to preserve the grip benefit while restoring compliance.

notes.title: Product documentation in context
paragraphs: Product documentation allows another person to understand, reproduce, use or maintain an outcome. Its contents depend on the task: dimensions and materials support making, while labelled controls and ordered instructions support use. Record versions so instructions correspond to the actual product. Distinguish a design drawing from an as-built record when changes occurred during creation. Photographs can help, but an image without scale or explanation may conceal essential details. A useful handover includes known limits and the evidence behind performance claims.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional handover for a card stand includes a photograph but no dimensions or assembly sequence. Specify a better package.
steps: Add a dimensioned drawing, materials list and numbered assembly steps with orientation cues.
Include the tested version, a photo of the assembled stand and any use limits found during evaluation.
workedExamples.conclusion: The documentation should let another person reproduce and use the same version without guessing from the photograph.

flashcards.front: What is an as-built record?
flashcards.back: Documentation of what was actually made, including changes from the plan.

flashcards.front: Why label a documentation version?
flashcards.back: Instructions must match the product being used.

flashcards.front: What can a photograph omit?
flashcards.back: Scale, dimensions, hidden joints and the order of assembly.

flashcards.front: What should accompany a performance claim?
flashcards.back: The relevant test conditions and results.

diagrams.title: Product documentation: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Making information → Use information → Traceability. Version records link the guidance to the tested outcome.

edges.label: A reproducible object still needs clear use guidance.
Version records link the guidance to the tested outcome.

additionalPractice.prompt: A drawing says 180 mm, but the final product measures 170 mm. What should the handover record?
solution: Record 170 mm as the actual dimension.
Retain the original plan as history if useful, clearly labelled.
Explain why the change occurred and whether the revised product met its requirement.
successCriteria: Record 170 mm as the actual dimension.
Retain the original plan as history if useful, clearly labelled.
Explain why the change occurred and whether the revised product met its requirement.

additionalPractice.prompt: An instruction says “attach this there”. Improve its information content.
solution: Name the two parts using labels that match the diagram.
State the attachment location and orientation.
Specify the method or fastener and where the step belongs in the assembly sequence.
successCriteria: Name the two parts using labels that match the diagram.
State the attachment location and orientation.
Specify the method or fastener and where the step belongs in the assembly sequence.

notes.title: Criterion A in context
paragraphs: Inquiry and analysis should establish why a design problem matters and what evidence will guide the response. A brief should emerge from research rather than merely restating a favourite idea. Distinguish primary findings from secondary information, and analyse existing products in relation to the user’s need. A research plan prioritises questions whose answers affect decisions. Explain limitations such as a small sample or a different user context. These editorial exercises practise inquiry reasoning; use the current school task and subject guidance for formal assessment requirements.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional finding: six of nine club members miss schedule changes because updates appear on three different boards. Develop an inquiry direction.
steps: The evidence suggests a problem of locating consistent current information, not necessarily a need for an app.
Investigate where members check first, who updates each board and how outdated notices are removed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The inquiry should clarify information flow and user habits before selecting a communication solution.

flashcards.front: What should inquiry establish?
flashcards.back: The need, context and evidence relevant to a design response.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes primary and secondary research?
flashcards.back: Primary research gathers direct evidence; secondary research uses existing sources.

flashcards.front: Why prioritise research questions?
flashcards.back: Some answers affect design decisions more directly than others.

flashcards.front: What should a research-based brief explain?
flashcards.back: The problem, users, constraints and evidence informing the proposed direction.

diagrams.title: Criterion A: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Finding → Analysis → Research direction. The analysis determines which questions need answers.

nodes.label: Finding
nodes.detail: Updates are spread across three boards.

nodes.label: Research direction
nodes.detail: Trace checking habits and update responsibility.

edges.label: The observation suggests an information-flow problem.
The analysis determines which questions need answers.

additionalPractice.prompt: A learner collects ten pictures of products but explains none. What analysis would make the research useful?
hints: Connect features to the user need.
solution: Identify which features address the stated problem.
Explain strengths and weaknesses in the intended context.
Use the comparison to derive requirements or research questions rather than treating image collection as analysis.
successCriteria: Identify which features address the stated problem.
Explain strengths and weaknesses in the intended context.
Use the comparison to derive requirements or research questions rather than treating image collection as analysis.

additionalPractice.prompt: A research plan asks users their favourite colour before checking whether a device fits the available space. Evaluate the priority.
solution: Available space may determine whether a concept is feasible.
Colour preference is usually secondary unless the brief makes it critical.
Measure the space and essential use needs first, then investigate visual preferences.
successCriteria: Available space may determine whether a concept is feasible.
Colour preference is usually secondary unless the brief makes it critical.
Measure the space and essential use needs first, then investigate visual preferences.

notes.title: Criterion B in context
paragraphs: Developing ideas requires a visible connection between research, specifications and proposed solutions. A sketch should communicate enough detail for a reader to understand how the concept works. Explain why a chosen idea responds to the criteria, including its compromises, rather than selecting it only because it looks attractive. Planning drawings and diagrams need relevant dimensions or relationships. If evidence is uncertain, identify what a prototype must test. These exercises support design reasoning but do not substitute for the school’s current assessment rubric.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional brief: a notice holder must be under 150 mm wide and keep text visible. A is 145 mm with a clear front; B is 140 mm with a decorative panel covering the lower text. Compare.
steps: Both concepts satisfy the width limit.
Only A satisfies the stated visibility requirement without revision; B’s decoration obstructs information.
workedExamples.conclusion: Choose A provisionally on the supplied criteria, then test actual readability rather than relying on the sketch alone.

flashcards.front: What should connect an idea to research?
flashcards.back: Specifications derived from the need and evidence.

flashcards.front: What makes a sketch useful?
flashcards.back: It communicates function, arrangement and relevant dimensions or relationships.

flashcards.front: Why explain compromises?
flashcards.back: A chosen idea may satisfy some preferences better than others.

flashcards.front: What follows uncertainty in a design drawing?
flashcards.back: A targeted prototype test.

diagrams.title: Criterion B: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Specifications → Comparison → Justified choice. The comparison supplies the reason for selection.

nodes.label: Comparison
nodes.detail: Both fit; only A keeps all text visible.

nodes.label: Justified choice
nodes.detail: A is the stronger candidate for testing.

edges.label: The same requirements are applied to both concepts.
The comparison supplies the reason for selection.

additionalPractice.prompt: A learner chooses a concept because “blue is my favourite”. Improve the justification for a public information sign.
hints: Use user needs rather than personal preference alone.
solution: Compare legibility and contrast in the intended setting.
Use user research and the information hierarchy to justify choices.
Personal preference can be acknowledged but should not replace evidence that the sign communicates effectively.
successCriteria: Compare legibility and contrast in the intended setting.
Use user research and the information hierarchy to justify choices.
Personal preference can be acknowledged but should not replace evidence that the sign communicates effectively.

additionalPractice.prompt: A drawing shows a fold but no direction or location. What should be added before making?
solution: Mark the fold line at a measured location.
Indicate which way the material folds.
Add labels or a sequence view so another maker can reproduce the intended form.
successCriteria: Mark the fold line at a measured location.
Indicate which way the material folds.
Add labels or a sequence view so another maker can reproduce the intended form.

notes.title: Criterion C in context
paragraphs: Creation involves carrying out a plan while documenting changes and checking quality. A useful plan identifies dependencies: a part cannot be assembled before it is prepared, and a fit check may prevent wasted work later. Time estimates should include checks, not only making. If the plan changes, record the reason and effect rather than rewriting history as if the change were always intended. Evidence of technical skill should show the process and resulting quality. Classroom making must follow the teacher’s tool and material procedures.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional card model plan: measure 6 minutes, mark 7, prepare pieces 9, assemble 11, check 7. Calculate the total and place a dimension check.
steps: Total time is 6 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 7 = 40 minutes.
Check marked dimensions before preparing pieces, since an error is easier to correct before material is altered.
workedExamples.conclusion: The plan includes 40 minutes of activity and a useful early checkpoint rather than leaving all checks until the end.

flashcards.front: What is a dependency?
flashcards.back: An activity that must happen before another can proceed.

flashcards.front: Why include checks in a making plan?
flashcards.back: They take time and can prevent later rework.

flashcards.front: How should an unplanned change be recorded?
flashcards.back: State what changed, why and how it affected the outcome.

flashcards.front: What governs classroom tool use?
flashcards.back: The teacher’s applicable procedures and supervision.

diagrams.title: Criterion C: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Plan → Checkpoint → Creation record. The check informs whether making can proceed as planned.

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.detail: Measure and mark before preparing pieces.

nodes.label: Creation record
nodes.detail: Document assembly and any justified changes.

edges.label: The dependency determines the sequence.
The check informs whether making can proceed as planned.

additionalPractice.prompt: A plan allocates 8, 12, 15 and 5 minutes to four sequential stages. Find the total and explain why parallel timing would be wrong if each depends on the previous stage.
solution: The total is 8 + 12 + 15 + 5 = 40 minutes.
Each stage must wait for the previous one.
The durations cannot be overlapped under that dependency assumption.
successCriteria: The total is 8 + 12 + 15 + 5 = 40 minutes.

additionalPractice.prompt: A maker changes a joint after a fit problem but omits the change from the log. Explain what to add.
solution: Record the fit problem observed.
Describe the revised joint and why it was chosen.
Add the subsequent fit check so the effect of the change can be assessed.
successCriteria: Record the fit problem observed.
Describe the revised joint and why it was chosen.
Add the subsequent fit check so the effect of the change can be assessed.

notes.title: Criterion D in context
paragraphs: Evaluating a design requires evidence matched to the specifications and a reasoned account of its impact on users. State the test method clearly enough to interpret the result. A comparison before and after a revision can suggest improvement, but different participants or conditions limit causal certainty. Explain realistic improvements in relation to particular failures. Distinguish whether a requirement was met in a small trial from whether the product will work for everyone. These exercises practise evaluation reasoning rather than awarding official criterion levels.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional target: five of six users find a card within 25 seconds unaided. V1 records four successes; v2 records five with a new group. Evaluate.
steps: V2 meets the stated five-of-six threshold in its trial, while v1 did not.
The groups differ, so the increase cannot be attributed solely to the revision.
workedExamples.conclusion: Report that v2 met the criterion under the tested conditions and propose a comparable follow-up if a stronger causal claim is needed.

flashcards.front: What anchors design evaluation?
flashcards.back: Pre-set specifications and recorded test evidence.

flashcards.front: Why note different participant groups?
flashcards.back: Group differences may affect results independently of the design.

flashcards.front: What makes an improvement proposal useful?
flashcards.back: It targets a specific weakness and explains how it could help.

flashcards.front: Does one passing trial prove universal success?
flashcards.back: No; report the tested conditions and remaining limits.

diagrams.title: Criterion D: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Evidence → Criterion → Qualified evaluation. Different groups limit the stronger causal interpretation.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.detail: V2 records five unaided successes out of six.

nodes.label: Qualified evaluation
nodes.detail: The trial passes; the cause of change remains uncertain.

edges.label: The result can be judged against the threshold.
Different groups limit the stronger causal interpretation.

additionalPractice.prompt: A test has no recorded task or conditions but concludes “users found it easy”. What is missing?
solution: The task and testing conditions are unspecified.
There is no clear measure or threshold for ease.
Record user comments alongside a defined task and observable success criteria before making a strong usability claim.
successCriteria: The task and testing conditions are unspecified.
There is no clear measure or threshold for ease.
Record user comments alongside a defined task and observable success criteria before making a strong usability claim.

additionalPractice.prompt: A product meets dimensions but two users cannot read its labels. Propose a justified improvement and test.
solution: Revise label size, contrast or wording based on the observed difficulty.
Retest reading with the intended users at the specified distance.
Recheck dimensions or layout if the larger labels alter the product.
